profile.summary: ProtTrans is a family of protein language models from Rostlab, trained on unlabelled protein sequences from UniRef and BFD. The models take an amino acid sequence and return per-residue vectors (1024 values each for ProtT5-XL), which are averaged for a per-protein vector; those vectors are then used as the only input to small supervised models for tasks such as secondary structure or subcellular localisation. The family covers six architectures, and ProtT5-XL-UniRef50 is the one the authors recommend.

The model could be used for protein feature extraction or to be fine-tuned on downstream tasks.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Each model is a standard NLP transformer trained on protein sequences with no labels. The authors trained two autoregressive models (Transformer-XL and XLNet) and four autoencoder models (BERT, Albert, Electra and T5). ProtT5-XL-UniRef50 follows the t5-3b shape, with model width 1024, 24 encoder and 24 decoder layers and 32 heads, but is trained with a Bart-like masked language modelling objective rather than T5 span denoising, masking 15% of amino acids. Sequences are uppercased, the rare amino acids U, Z, O and B are mapped to X, and residues are separated by single spaces. For feature extraction the authors recommend the encoder side only.
sections.source_locator: arXiv abstract; model card: Model description, Preprocessing; config.json

quotes.text: we trained two auto-regressive models (Transformer-XL, XLNet) and four auto-encoder models (BERT, Albert, Electra, T5) on data from UniRef and BFD containing up to 393 billion amino acids
ProtT5-XL-UniRef50 is based on the `t5-3b` model and was pretrained on a large corpus of protein sequences in a self-supervised fashion.
The original T5-3B model was pretrained using a span denosing objective, while this model was pre-trained with a Bart-like MLM denosing objective.
The masking probability is consistent with the original T5 training by randomly masking 15% of the amino acids in the input.
The protein sequences are uppercased and tokenized using a single space and a vocabulary size of 21. The rare amino acids "U,Z,O,B" were mapped to "X".
for feature extraction, its better to use the feature extracted from the encoder not from the decoder

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The README lists ten checkpoints on Hugging Face and Zenodo: ProtT5-XL-UniRef50, ProtT5-XL-BFD, ProtT5-XXL-UniRef50, ProtT5-XXL-BFD, ProtBert-BFD, ProtBert, ProtAlbert, ProtXLNet, ProtElectra-Generator-BFD and ProtElectra-Discriminator-BFD. There is also Rostlab/prot_t5_xl_half_uniref50-enc, a half-precision encoder-only copy of ProtT5-XL-UniRef50 used in the README example. The training corpus differs between the UniRef50 and BFD variants, so a result must name the checkpoint. The Hugging Face API responses carry no parameter counts and no licence field, so the revision is the only version handle; this page read prot_t5_xl_uniref50 at revision 973be27c.

run_guide.summary: Install the Python libraries and compute per-residue and per-protein embeddings for two short sequences with the ProtT5-XL half-precision encoder.
prerequisites: Python with pip, PyTorch and the transformers library.
A GPU is optional; the README says CPU needs full precision and is much slower.
Internet access to Hugging Face for the checkpoint.
The weights are under the Academic Free License v3.0.

steps.title: Install
steps.shell:
pip install torch
pip install transformers
pip install sentencepiece
pip install protobuf
steps.explanation: The README's install commands. protobuf is listed as the fix for an UnboundLocalError raised by recent versions of the T5 tokenizer.

steps.title: Embed two sequences
steps.shell:
python3 - <<'PY'
from transformers import T5Tokenizer, T5EncoderModel
import torch
import re

device = torch.device('cuda:0' if torch.cuda.is_available() else 'cpu')

tokenizer = T5Tokenizer.from_pretrained('Rostlab/prot_t5_xl_half_uniref50-enc', do_lower_case=False)
model = T5EncoderModel.from_pretrained("Rostlab/prot_t5_xl_half_uniref50-enc").to(device)

if device == torch.device("cpu"):
    model.to(torch.float32)

sequence_examples = ["PRTEINO", "SEQWENCE"]
sequence_examples = [" ".join(list(re.sub(r"[UZOB]", "X", sequence))) for sequence in sequence_examples]

ids = tokenizer(sequence_examples, add_special_tokens=True, padding="longest")

input_ids = torch.tensor(ids['input_ids']).to(device)
attention_mask = torch.tensor(ids['attention_mask']).to(device)

with torch.no_grad():
    embedding_repr = model(input_ids=input_ids, attention_mask=attention_mask)

emb_0 = embedding_repr.last_hidden_state[0,:7] # shape (7 x 1024)
emb_1 = embedding_repr.last_hidden_state[1,:8] # shape (8 x 1024)
emb_0_per_protein = emb_0.mean(dim=0) # shape (1024)
print(emb_0.shape, emb_0_per_protein.shape)
PY
steps.explanation: The README's Quick Start example, wrapped in a shell heredoc by Rewire, with its comments shortened and a print of the two shapes added at the end.

steps.title: Embed a FASTA file
steps.shell:
python prott5_embedder.py --input sequences/some.fasta --output embeddings/residue_embeddings.h5
python prott5_embedder.py --input sequences/some.fasta --output embeddings/protein_embeddings.h5 --per_protein 1
steps.explanation: The repository's embedding script, which writes per-residue or per-protein embeddings for a FASTA file to an HDF5 file. The script lives in the Embedding folder of the repository.

outputs: The heredoc prints the two tensor shapes: 7 by 1024 residue embeddings and a 1024-value per-protein embedding. The script writes an HDF5 file of embeddings.
